purpose_text: DETAIL, STRENGTH. Combines pulling power and arm speed. Helps increase tempo, but is difficult, so perform it in short bursts.
how: Swim backstroke with a dolphin kick. Use one kick per stroke. Swimmers must first find the rhythm; once established, the drill is effective for increasing tempo.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Helps correct an excessively flat body position and encourages greater side-to-side rotation.
how: Take 2 strokes with the right arm, 2 with the left arm, and then 3 strokes with both arms to transition to the other side. The stationary arm stays down during the single-arm strokes. Focus on side-to-side upper-body rotation during those strokes. Use fins.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Helps flatten excessive vertical body movement, teaches the swimmer to push water backward rather than downward or sideways, and improves kick strength while swimming.
how: Swim backstroke with both arms moving together and use a regular backstroke kick. This forces the legs to work harder because the arms do not provide support during recovery.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Helps keep the head steady and the eyes directed toward the ceiling.
how: Fill a cup with water, and then kick, drill, or swim backstroke while balancing the object on your forehead. Tip: Use rubber ducks or paddles instead of cups.

purpose_text: DETAIL, STRENGTH. Develops arm speed. This drill teaches the body to turn over at a rate higher than race tempo to improve stroke rate.
how: Sit upright in the water as though sitting in a chair; your eyes should look back toward the end of the pool from which you pushed off. Rotate the arms as quickly as possible. Focus only on achieving the highest possible tempo rather than on technique. This drill develops tempo, not correct body position.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Works on whole-body rotation rather than trunk rotation alone. Uses backstroke kicking only.
how: Perform a backstroke kick with both arms down while rotating the body from side to side. Do not move erratically or force the rotation at first. Learn to control the body and maintain the kick from the back and at different side angles. Initiate the rotation from the hips, and move slowly and deliberately. Add faster rotations only after maintaining body alignment. Keep the head still and the eyes directed toward the ceiling.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Works on finding a high body position in which the hips, shoulders, and chin remain at the surface without any part feeling submerged. The switch version adds movement to improve kinesthetic awareness.
how: One arm extends straight overhead underwater; the other arm extends toward the ceiling while the body rotates to the side along its long axis. Work on balancing and applying pressure through the submerged forward arm so that the body position stays high and the hip remains at the surface. In the switch version, change arms every 6 kicks rather than completing the entire lap with the same arm raised.

purpose_text: STRENGTH. Works on a strong flutter kick and proper body position.
how: Hold a kickboard with both arms either vertically or at a 45-degree angle above the head. Use fins for beginners and no fins for more advanced swimmers. The goal is to develop a strong kick that maintains proper body position.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Develops the feel of the finishing scull during the final part of the stroke.
how: Scull near the hips while using a buoy or floating without active kicking. This forces you to push backward with the hands strongly enough to move forward, thereby emphasizing the final underwater part of the stroke. Use both hands together or one hand at a time.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Working on underwater catch and maintaining strong kick/body position, especially while on the side during pull.
how: This differs slightly from freestyle catch-up. One arm points toward the ceiling while the other completes a full rotation; the catch-up occurs when both arms are vertical. Use fins because maintaining a high body position is difficult while one arm is extended upward.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL. Helps bring the shoulder out of the water.
how: This drill is easier with fins. Keep one arm down by the side and point the other arm toward the ceiling. Rotate the body and extend the upward-pointing arm as far out of the water as possible, and then lower it again. The goal is to bring the shoulder out while rotating the body and return it while the body is flat. Switch sides on the next lap.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Uses the forearm and practices early vertical forearm (EVF).
how: Swim backstroke with closed fists so that you rely less on the hands for propulsion and can feel the movement of the entire arm.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Works on bending the arm rather than pulling with a straight arm.
how: Swim regular backstroke, but intentionally allow the fingers or hand to emerge slightly while pushing backward, creating a small backward splash at the end of the pull. Focus on bending the elbow. Avoid overusing the drill or teaching children to keep the fingers out during the final part of the pull.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Reinforces the correct arm and hand pulling motion for backstroke and allows the swimmer to feel an exaggerated version of the force used in a strong backstroke pull.
how: Perform a single-arm backstroke drill. During the pull, the arm closest to the lane line catches the lane-line discs and pulls along the line until the body passes, requiring release before the next stroke begins. Do not lead with the elbow while pulling; maintain an elbow angle of 100-130 degrees.

warnings.reason: Pulling on the lane line may create a risk of finger entrapment, sudden lane-line tension, or collision with other pool users. A coach should confirm that the lane setup, surrounding space, and level of supervision are appropriate before using this drill.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. This drill isolates the pulling pattern. Perform it with attention to balanced body position, rotation, and a steady tempo. It is an effective way to understand the underwater arm action in backstroke.
how: Keep the non-working arm at your side, begin the pull with a deep catch, and rotate to both sides. Each shoulder should emerge from the water according to the position of the working arm: the opposite shoulder when the arm is up and the same-side shoulder when the arm is down. Move slowly and focus on the arm shape during every pull and recovery. Maintain a steady kick and a stable body position.

warnings.reason: The instructions to begin with a deep catch and expose both shoulders at different stages should be reviewed for compatibility with the swimmer's shoulder mobility and with the backstroke rotation technique being taught.

purpose_text: STRENGTH, DETAIL. Reinforces the importance of continuous kicking.
how: Hold a buoy and move it with straight arms in a half-circle above the water from streamline to the hips while kicking. From the side, the movement resembles tracing a rainbow. Use fins with swimmers who have weaker kicks.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops awareness of the arm-entry angle.
how: Give the swimmer a sense of the arm angle used for hand entry. Swim backstroke while entering the hands at 12 o’clock, then at 11 and 1 o’clock, and then at 10 and 2 o’clock; repeat for 25-50 yards. This allows swimmers to experience different interpretations of the “11 and 1” entry.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL. To find the line between efficiency and tempo.
how: Swim backstroke, alternating between 2 cycles focused on establishing a strong catch and 2 cycles focused on arm speed.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER, PROGRESSION. This drill develops awareness of rotation by checking: 1) whether the head remains still; 2) whether the shoulders and hips rotate together; 3) whether the kick remains strong; and 4) the stroke tempo.
how: Take 3 normal backstroke strokes, and then pause on the side for 6 kicks. Keep one hand at the hip and the other above the head in the catch position, with the palm down and the body rotated to the side. After 6 kicks, take 3 strokes again and pause for 6 kicks on the opposite side. Begin slowly, and then add speed. Perform this drill after the 6 Kick Switch and 1 Stroke + 6 Kicks drills as a progression toward full-stroke swimming.

purpose_text: DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Goal is to work on stretching out the stroke.
how: After the push-off, pull one arm down to the side and hold the position: the front arm extends forward, the rear arm extends behind, the rear shoulder remains out of the water, and the body rotates to the side. Hold for 3 seconds, take a stroke, and then hold for 3 seconds with the opposite arm raised.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER, PROGRESSION. Suitable for swimmers of all levels. Works on rotation and continuous kicking.
how: Kick on the back with the arms by the sides. Rotate the body from side to side while keeping the head still and the eyes directed toward the ceiling. Begin with slow rotations, and then increase the rotation speed. Use fins if desired. Follow with the 1 Stroke + 6 Kicks and 3 Strokes + 6 Kicks drills.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER, PROGRESSION. Suitable for swimmers of all levels. Works on rotation, continuous kicking, the catch, and speed.
how: Take 1 normal backstroke stroke, and then pause on the side for 6 kicks. Keep one hand at the hip and the other above the head in the catch position, with the palm down and the body rotated to the side. After 6 kicks, take 1 stroke with the other arm and pause for 6 kicks on the opposite side. Begin slowly, and then add speed. Perform this drill after the 6 Kick Switch, and follow it with the 3 Strokes + 6 Kicks drill as a progression toward full-stroke swimming.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Allows the swimmer to focus on the pull pattern, hand placement, and shoulder rotation. This is more advanced because the swimmer must maintain the pattern and a strong kick; fins may be used for assistance.
how: Pause for 2 seconds as one hand enters the water after recovery, and wait for the other hand to catch up. Continue with one-arm pulls, and then kick for 6 kicks with the arms at the sides before beginning again. Start with the other hand on the next repetition.

purpose_text: STRENGTH. Focuses on core and kick strength, balance, and body position. This drill is best suited to older, more experienced swimmers. Swimmers with weak kicks or insufficient core stability may sink underwater. Poor body position may also cause the swimmer to sink.
how: Kick backstroke with the hands together in a streamline directed straight upward toward the ceiling rather than in the water, forming an arrow pointing out of the water. The original description states that the streamline should be at 90 degrees to the upward-extending hands. Swimmers must keep the head back in the water and engage the core to remain at the surface with a flat body position. Use fins with beginners.

warnings.reason: The original reference for the phrase '90 degrees to the hands' is unclear. The intended angle relative to the water surface, arms, hands, and body should be confirmed before instruction.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops an understanding of the catch and is better suited to older children.
how: Keep 1 arm up and 1 arm down with the body flat. As the catch begins, roll the shoulder opposite the catching arm upward. Establish the catch, but return the catching arm to the raised position from approximately the shoulder line instead of pushing it fully down. Return the arm to streamline and roll the body back to a flat position.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. The movement pattern takes some practice, but it develops body awareness in younger swimmers. It maintains core stability and engages the kick while focusing on rotation and the mechanics of the backstroke recovery from start to finish.
how: One arm begins in the catch position above the head while the other arm starts at the hip. Raise the lower arm to 90 degrees, lower it back to the hip, and then raise it again, this time finishing in the catch position as the opposite arm performs a pull. Repeat on the opposite side after the arm positions switch. Move slowly so that you can observe the movement.

purpose_text: DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Body rotation and underwater pull improvements.
how: This drill follows naturally from the rotating kick drill. Kick with the arms down while rotating from side to side, and then add the arm action. Instead of recovering the arms over the water, slide each arm forward underwater close to the body and perform a full catch and pull to return the arm to the side. This encourages a rotated position at the start of the pull as the hand slides forward underwater.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. An anti-bicycling drill that teaches swimmers to prevent the knees from emerging excessively during the kick.
how: Perform backstroke kicks while holding a kickboard with straight arms extended toward the feet so that the board covers the knees. Focus on keeping the knees from contacting the board.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION, DETAIL. Connects the alternating kick to the finishing phase of the underwater pull. This supports timing and core connection.
how: Kick on the side with the arms by the sides and the elbows close to the body. With the lower arm, establish the catch and finish the push while using that action to connect the core and rotate to the other side. Finish the push with the palm facing down, and do not begin the recovery too early.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, DETAIL. Hand exit and entry positions, relaxing the arm during recovery.
how: Exit thumb-first and transition to a little-finger-first entry while adding a small wave-like hand movement during recovery, when the arm is vertical and the shoulder is out of the water.

purpose_text: STRENGTH, DETAIL. Develops shoulder rotation and extension, kick power, and a straight-arm recovery position. Simulates the start of the catch. This is a more advanced variation of the Extension Drill.
how: Begin with fins. Keep the shoulders flat, with one arm fully extended overhead in the catch position, little finger down, and the other arm at 90 degrees toward the ceiling while holding a full water bottle. Kick down the pool continuously while slowly rotating the shoulders and pressing the water bottle toward the ceiling until the shoulder approaches the chin and the palm of the extended hand turns slightly farther downward. Then return slowly to a flat position. Repeat with the other arm on the next lap.

warnings.reason: Holding a water bottle above the surface while performing backstroke kick may increase shoulder strain and create a dropped-object hazard. Supervision and equipment suitability should be confirmed.

purpose_text: DETAIL. This drill focuses heavily on body alignment and rotation. By eliminating the arm coming out of the water it forces the swimmer to actually turn their body to the side earlier/more and not stay flat on their back. For more advanced swimmers.
how: Push off flat on the back while kicking with both hands at the sides. Reach one hand overhead while keeping it fully submerged. Once the hand is above the head, rotate the body to the side until the opposite shoulder emerges from the water, and then pause for a 4-second kick. Complete the pull and push through the water. Switch arms every stroke or repeat with one arm for the entire lap.

purpose_text: STRENGTH, DETAIL. Develops arm speed and maintains straight arms during recovery while also working on kick strength and core stability.
how: Practice the recovery phase only. While kicking with fins, either tap the hands or fingers together above the water or move the arms in a scissor-like pattern above and below; do not perform an underwater pull. Move quickly to increase arm speed and backstroke tempo. The hands should contact the water as far above the head and below the hips as possible, encouraging straight arms during recovery. The movement may feel unfamiliar, but it can be used as a variation.

warnings.reason: The instruction to tap the hands above and below or move them in a scissor pattern can be interpreted in several spatial directions. The intended hand path and range of motion should be clarified before use.

purpose_text: STRENGTH, APPRECIATION. Strengthens the shoulders and core for backstroke while developing feel for the water.
how: The swimmer floats on the back, and then brings the chest and legs toward one another to form a V position. The toes and shoulders should remain out of the water while the swimmer sculls backward. This drill works the core, shoulders, and neck. For assistance, swimmers may place a pull buoy between the feet or thighs to help lift the toes while maintaining focus on the core. Gradually straighten the body during the lap to emphasize a flat position during regular swimming.

warnings.reason: Maintaining a V-shaped position can place sustained tension on the neck and shoulders. The swimmer's cervical and shoulder tolerance, as well as the duration of the drill, should be checked.

purpose_text: DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Body balance and position, plus feel of the water and arm position above the head.
how: Place the hands above the head and scull with small hand movements while keeping the elbows straight and moving feet-first. This requires core engagement to maintain a flat body position, prevent the feet from sinking, and develop awareness of the arm position above the head. This drill is better suited to more experienced swimmers.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, ESSENTIAL. A basic drill for achieving body alignment with the hips and feet high in the water.
how: Kick on the back with the hands extended straight overhead in streamline. Focus on small, fast kicks and keeping the legs and hips high. Keep the head low in the water. Every few kicks, briefly lower the face slightly underwater so that a small flow passes over it, practicing head alignment and the slight upward position of the back and hips as the hand enters at the end of recovery.

warnings.reason: Briefly submerging the face while arching the back and hips upward may encourage excessive lumbar extension. A coach should confirm that a neutral, controlled body line is maintained.

purpose_text: DETAIL, ESSENTIAL. To practice bent arm pulling motion and rotation.
how: Swim with one arm while keeping the other arm down by the side. Alternate between one freestyle pull and one backstroke pull. Rotate to one side only: the side opposite the freestyle pulling arm and the same side as the backstroke pulling arm. This encourages rotation and greater elbow flexion. Alternate arms every 25 or 50.

purpose_text: To practice the backstroke start step by step.
how:
Sink down, push off, and float on the back as far as possible. Keep the eyes directed toward the sky and the body straight like an arrow.
After the streamline float is mastered, add a minimum of 5 dolphin kicks.
After the kicks are consistent, add more amplitude. Hold the pool edge rather than the block, with the feet approximately 2 feet below the surface. Push off, swing the arms overhead and behind, lift the hips, and enter the water hands-first after briefly clearing the surface or traveling just above it.
Move to the starting block, grasp the bar, and position the feet so that the toes are just below the waterline. Repeat the previous step while moving into streamline and performing underwater dolphin kicks (UDK).

warnings.reason: This progression uses the pool wall to create an airborne phase before a hands-first entry. Pool depth, wall structure, deck conditions, and direct supervision must be confirmed.

Fixing the feet approximately 2 feet below the surface and emphasizing a large arch may not suit every swimmer's body dimensions or facility setup. The foot position and arch amplitude should be individualized.

purpose_text: Teaches forward propulsion, leg extension, and lifting the hips above the water.
how: Push off as in a normal start, but enter hips-first in a seated position with the arms and legs extended straight backward.

warnings.reason: An intentional buttocks-first entry may transmit impact to the lower back or tailbone. Water depth, entry height, and drill intensity should be carefully controlled.

purpose_text: Develops a high leg position and reaction speed.
how: Use a volleyball or a softer object. Hold it above the swimmer’s legs; as the swimmer pushes off, the swimmer kicks the ball out of the instructor’s hands with the feet. For a more advanced variation, drop the ball from slightly higher on the “Go” signal, and have the swimmer react quickly enough to kick it before it reaches the water.

warnings.reason: Holding or dropping a ball above the swimmer's legs may create contact risk to the swimmer's face or the coach's hands and may interfere with adjacent lanes. Clear space and direct supervision are required.

name_en: DIVE OVER KICK BOARD/POOL NOODLE/PHYSIO BALL
purpose_text: Develops a high arch during the start.
how: Hold the physio ball or other object behind the swimmer. During the start, the swimmer clears the object, preferably without touching it. Perform this drill only in the deep end of the pool.

warnings.reason: Clearing a ball, kickboard, or noodle during a backstroke start may create collision and shallow-entry hazards. Use only in a dedicated area with adequate depth and direct supervision.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, PROGRESSION. For young swimmers learning the basic steps.
how:
1. Kick with a board to practice the kick.
2. Kick without a board to practice streamline and lifting the legs after the kick.
3. Kick with a small scull to practice quick head movement.
4. Kick with a ¾ pull to ensure that the elbows do not travel too far backward.
5. Full breaststroke.
 Focus throughout on returning the head to the water as soon as possible, entering streamline, separating the pull from the kick, and maintaining the glide after each kick.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Keeping knees narrow.
how: Kick, perform drills, or swim with a band above the knees so that the knees cannot move much wider than shoulder width. Try the 2 Kicks 1 Pull drill.

warnings.reason: A band placed above the knees may cause excessive compression, skin irritation, or accidental release. Band tension, placement, circulation, and equipment condition should be checked before use.

name_en: 2-3 KICK DOWN DRILL aka. 2 KICKS 1 PULL
purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Develops entry into streamline and maintenance of streamline after the kick.
how: Perform 1 pull followed by 2-3 kicks underwater in a complete racing streamline. Remain underwater for the kicks. This can be part of a sequence, for example: 8*75 with 25 using 1P:3K, 25 using 1P:2K, and 25 using 1P:1K.

warnings.reason: Repeating 2-3 breaststroke kicks underwater after one pull differs from the underwater actions permitted in competition breaststroke. The drill should be clearly identified as training-only.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Reinforces the breaststroke sequence, correct timing, and the importance of the glide.
how: Say “chicken,” or count to 3 before beginning the next pull. Say it only when the hands are in front, not before.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Works on the kick and streamline.
how: Perform the drill on the stomach, on the back, or underwater. Maintain a racing streamline with the elbows close together and the head low between the arms when not breathing. Keep the knees narrow, approximately shoulder-width apart, both while driving the kick backward and while recovering the legs forward. When performing breaststroke kick on the back, allowing the knees to approach the surface may help the swimmer observe the position of the feet, hips, and shoulders and restore a flat body position before the next kick. Also focus on fully extending the legs, lifting them, and pointing the toes at the end of each kick so that the swimmer returns to a flat streamline. Perform the movement without rushing.

warnings.reason: Allowing the knees to emerge during breaststroke kick on the back, while also requiring the feet, hips, and shoulders to remain level, may not suit all body types. The intended alignment should be reviewed and individualized.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Works on knee placement during the kick and flexibility.
how: Place the hands directly above the hips. Touch the hands with the heels on every kick. The closer the hands are to one another, the narrower the heel recovery must be. Begin with the hands at the sides. Perform the drill on the stomach or back, and return to a flat body position after every kick.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Helps prevent young swimmers from pulling the elbows too far backward.
how: Swim or pull with a pool noodle positioned under the chin and armpits. Move slowly.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL. Develops rhythm, maintains a high body position, enhances pulling power, and practices late-breath timing.
how: Swim breaststroke with a butterfly kick. Perform 2 dolphin kicks per pull so that a short glide occurs during the second kick. Stay near the surface rather than diving downward. Fins may be used.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL. Focuses on the power and tempo of the pull.
how: Swim breaststroke with a flutter kick. Stay near the surface. Because the drill can be demanding, use fins and perform short lengths or repetitions.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Develops the glide and streamline.
how: Kick, pull, or swim 25s while counting the number of kicks, pulls, or strokes. Try to reduce the count on each subsequent length from wall to wall.

name_en: FRONT SCULL and STRAIGHT ARM SCULL
purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Develops early vertical forearm (EVF) and feel for the water.
how: Scull in front with both arms, keeping the little fingers directed outward as the hands move in both directions. Perform the movement slowly or quickly. Use a snorkel and, if needed, fins with younger swimmers so that they do not have to lift the head to breathe or allow the legs to sink; more advanced swimmers may use a pull buoy. As a variation, keep the arms fully straight to work on the earliest part of the stroke.

name_en: HEAD SLAM aka. KARATE CHOP aka. BREAK THE BOARD
purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Helps the swimmer return to streamline more quickly.
how: During the breaststroke pull, take a quick breath, return the face and forehead to the water promptly and under control, and then hold streamline briefly.

warnings.reason: The drill name and instruction encourage a rapid, forceful return of the face or forehead to the water. Coaching limits are needed to prevent cervical overflexion and impact-like movement.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Emphasizes the short-axis elements of both strokes, in which the body does not rotate side to side, and focuses on driving the body forward.
how: Perform 2 full butterfly strokes followed by 2 full breaststroke strokes. The goal is to learn to drive the head, neck, and shoulders forward in short-axis strokes with less fatigue. This drill is better suited to more advanced swimmers.

purpose_text: DETAIL, ESSENTIAL. A variation, or alternative explanation, of the “2 Kicks 1 Pull” drill that also promotes proper timing.
how: Allow each stroke to build into the next so that momentum is not lost. Instead of thinking of a single pull followed by 2 kicks, begin with a kick and flow into a full breaststroke cycle.

purpose_text: STRENGTH. Separates the kick to isolate the ankle and knee position of each leg and develops kinesthetic awareness of the kicking mechanics.
how: Perform the breaststroke kick with one leg at a time or alternate the legs. Perform the movements as quickly as control allows.

warnings.reason: Performing single-leg breaststroke kicks at maximum speed may create asymmetric loading at the medial knee, hip, and ankle. Range, speed, and repetition should be limited according to the swimmer's condition.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, DETAIL. Helps maintain a narrow kick.
how: Swim breaststroke with a pull buoy between the thighs. Young swimmers may use a kickboard to keep the upper body afloat.

warnings.reason: Maintaining a pull buoy between the thighs during breaststroke kick may alter the intended knee width and actual kick path. A coach should verify that the equipment supports rather than distorts the target movement.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Promotes arm speed at the end of the pull cycle.
how: Create a splash in front of the body at the end of the stroke phase.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops core strength and addresses asymmetries in the body.
how: Keep the opposite arm and leg in streamline while the working arm and leg complete the full range of the stroke and kick.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops timing and feel for the water while shortening the pull and reducing kick width.
how: Perform 2 breaststroke cycles at the surface followed by 2 cycles fully underwater. The drill is intended to narrow the kicks and prevent the elbows from traveling too far backward.

warnings.reason: Performing 2 complete breaststroke cycles underwater differs from competition-legal stroke execution and also increases breath-holding demand. Use only under controlled training conditions.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Teaches swimmers to glide in breaststroke and feel differences in glide duration.
how: Take 1 breaststroke stroke and glide for 3 seconds; on the next stroke, glide for 2 seconds; on the next, glide for 1 second; then repeat.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Separates the components of breaststroke.
how: Wear a snorkel and keep the head down. Think of “coiling with straight legs” and “kicking with straight arms” so that the decelerating portions of the stroke do not overlap. The hands travel only to the forehead while the kick remains complete; from above, the body should resemble an accordion.

warnings.reason: The terms 'negative acceleration parts,' 'coiling with straight legs,' and 'kicking with straight arms' are not defined in the document. The intended technical meanings should be confirmed before instruction.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, DETAIL. Provides a child-friendly cue for keeping the hips high and moving the head quickly.
how: Imagine a cobra striking. Begin with the hips high in the water, and then drive the head and arms forward quickly.

warnings.reason: The cobra analogy and rapid forward head action may encourage excessive cervical movement. A coach should limit the range and ensure that the motion is driven by the body rather than the neck alone.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Works on the catch phase, teaching the swimmer to hold the water and maintain a flat body position at the surface while moving feet-first.
how: Swimmers lie on the back and move forward feet-first by sculling simultaneously beside the hips.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Focus on use of hips in breaststroke. Hips anchor the movement.
how: While swimming breaststroke, raise the upper body at the top of the stroke as described, arch the back, and bring as much of the body out of the water as possible. Do not allow the hips to drop; lunge forward into the next stroke with the kick, and drive the hips back to the surface to re-establish the body line.

warnings.reason: Attempting to lift as much of the body out of the water as possible while arching the back may cause excessive lumbar extension. The height and spinal range should be limited.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Develops timing, especially for younger swimmers, by teaching that the breaststroke pull and kick are separate motions that require independent focus.
how: Separate the kick from the pull. With the legs straight, perform the breaststroke pull and return fully to a streamlined line. After the glide, keep the head aligned and the arms straight in front while performing the kick. Repeat slowly.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Develops acceleration through the stroke and teaches young swimmers to keep the arm action short rather than pulling to the hips.
how: Keep the head above the water and use a light flutter kick. Perform very fast half-length breaststroke arm actions. Keep the strokes small, driving the hands forward through the water and maintaining a high turnover rate. Use fins for assistance.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Alternating single-arm pulls teaches control of timing. Swimmers may slip through the stroke, pause at the chest with the pulling arm, or involve the non-pulling arm. Encourage continuous forward movement through each pull. After several cycles, swimmers should transfer the timing to the full breaststroke pull, developing greater timing awareness and a more effective pull.
how: Alternate a right-arm pull, a left-arm pull, and a full pull throughout the length. Use a full breaststroke kick after each pull. During each single-arm pull, keep the opposite arm extended in front. With the working arm, focus on establishing a secure catch at the beginning of the pull to feel forward propulsion. Move quickly through the middle and recovery phases while minimizing pauses.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Helps correct pulling the arms too far backward because the swimmer can see them more clearly, as light does not bend in the same way as at an air-water interface. Also helps with streamline.
how: Swim breaststroke on the back and underwater. This is an advanced drill and should be used sparingly. A nose clip may assist with comfort and breath control.

warnings.reason: Performing full breaststroke motions underwater while on the back may create breath-holding, orientation, and collision risks. Use only with experienced swimmers under direct supervision.
The claim that light does not refract underwater may be technically inaccurate. The visual-observation mechanism and instructional rationale should be reviewed before presenting it as an explanation.
Repeated underwater breaststroke cycles must be distinguished from the single competition-legal pullout sequence. The drill should be labeled as training-only.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Helps address a scissor kick or unintended dolphin kick in young swimmers.
how: In an end lane, have swimmers push off the wall with the foot during each kick. They may hold kickboards for support. Repeat on the other side when returning. The drill encourages use of the sole of the foot to press against the wall.

warnings.reason: Pushing forcefully from the wall with the feet on every kick may create ankle, knee, toe, or wall-contact impact. Use low intensity, adequate spacing, and controlled foot placement.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Focuses on body undulation and glide while using head movement to direct the body forward.
how: Place the arms in front of the head in a Y shape. Use a small scull to raise the head, and then direct the head downward while performing a kick. Allow the body to complete the undulating motion before resetting. Repeat without a full arm action, and complete the glide.

warnings.reason: Describing the head movement as driving the body forward may encourage excessive neck-led motion. A coach should confirm that propulsion remains coordinated through the trunk, arms, and kick.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, PROGRESSION. Dryland practice may help swimmers learn the complex kick pattern.
how:
Perform foot circles while seated with the legs straight: draw the toes upward, rotate the feet outward, and complete a circle.
While seated in a chair, bring the lower legs backward and around the chair legs; repeat.
Wall drill: Stand close to a wall and perform a single-leg kick while pushing off the wall. This helps keep the knees down and turn the toes outward.
Duck walks may also be used.

warnings.reason: Repeatedly pushing a wall with one leg may create asymmetric knee and ankle loading and may present a slipping hazard. Use stable footing and alternate or limit sides as appropriate.
Duck walking repeatedly combines deep knee flexion and rotation and may be unsuitable for swimmers with knee pain or restricted mobility. Screen participants and limit range and volume.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Develops timing, glide, and kick strength. For some swimmers, it also helps prevent the arms from spreading too wide.
how: Lock the thumbs together and keep them locked throughout the drill. Swim full breaststroke, drawing the elbows and hands inward while breathing, and recover the hands with the kick while keeping the thumbs locked.

purpose_text: STRENGTH. Develops leg strength and the ability to push water backward with the insteps and soles of the feet.
how: Keep the hands out of the water or overhead. Keeping the face above the water is difficult if the kick moves sideways or becomes excessively wide. Use this drill sparingly because it may interfere with finishing the kick with pointed toes and fully extended legs.

warnings.reason: Vertical breaststroke kicking can substantially increase breathing demand and loading at the knees and hips. Duration, water depth, flotation support, and swimmer level should be controlled.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Teaches whole-body kicking while keeping the head moving almost directly forward in a streamlined position, with the hands ideally moving no more than 3-4 inches above and below the line of travel. Keep the head between the biceps, or slightly below them for a narrower cross-section. A fast, efficient, and compact kick is the first building block of the stroke.
how:
Perform the kick on the stomach, back, or sides, with the arms up or down and with or without fins. Avoid relying on a kickboard because it may place pressure on the lower back and restrict natural body movement.
Note: Kicking on the side with the lower arm extended and the upper arm at the side is useful for practicing equal upward and downward kick actions because both directions require similar effort. Practicing on the back supports backstroke development, and rotating from side to side and from back to front supports fast turns.
Aim for 50-70 degrees of knee flexion and 20-30 degrees of hip flexion.

warnings.reason: The statement that kickboards generally place pressure on the lower back and restrict natural movement may not apply to every swimmer or board position. The claim should be treated as context-dependent.

Fixed ranges of 50-70 degrees of knee bend and 20-30 degrees of hip bend may not apply to every swimmer or every phase of the kick. The ranges should be reviewed biomechanically before being used as universal targets.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Teaches whole-body kicking and coordinated use of the core and back muscles, similar to a dolphin. It may also be described as moving with the water rather than resisting it.
how: Kick in a Superman position with the arms shoulder-width apart in front, focusing on each element of the kick. Keep the hands open at the surface. The movement may begin with a small motion at the fingertips and increase toward the feet, initiated by pressing the chest downward so that the hips rise. Keep the head near the surface and the eyes directed toward the pool bottom. The goal is to travel at or near the surface through an undulating motion in which the chest moves down, the hips rise, and the legs follow. The hips should approach the surface on each kick. Use a snorkel if desired or breathe forward. Fins should accentuate the feel of whole-body undulation rather than replace the kick. After mastering the drill on the stomach, perform it on the sides and back.

warnings.reason: Pressing the chest down so that the hips rise to the surface on every kick may encourage excessive vertical oscillation. A coach should confirm that the movement remains efficient and proportionate.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Helps younger swimmers learn this difficult stroke more easily and allows experienced swimmers to complete longer lengths or repetitions without losing body position or technique.
how: Swim butterfly with fins during longer sets or while learning to recover the arms smoothly in coordination with the kick. Do not use fins so extensively that the swimmer becomes dependent on them.

purpose_text: Develops timing, straight-arm recovery, and downward chest pressure.
how: Perform the drill with the resting arm either extended in front or held at the side. Keeping the resting arm at the side may interfere less with the natural movement and may support timing, although it is more difficult. Practice breathing both to the side and to the front: side breathing supports the recovery component and a flatter position, while front breathing practices chest pressure and head movement. Use fins to assist young swimmers.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Helps swimmers learn pull mechanics with less fatigue.
how: Alternate arms on each stroke, allowing the hands to meet in front. This is easier than full butterfly.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, DETAIL. Practices downward chest pressure.
how: Hold the arms wider in front to form a Y, keep them straight, and press the chest downward with each kick while the hands continue forward with the palms facing down. The kicks may be smaller than regular kicks. Use a snorkel for easier breathing. Move slowly.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Develops the timing of the kicks and pull. The drill is named after Matt Biondi, who won 11 Olympic medals, including 8 gold medals, 25 years before Phelps.
how: Build speed with several dolphin kicks, and then perform a full arm pull, stopping with the hands at the sides. Lower the head as the second kick occurs, and glide briefly with the arms at the sides. A breath may be taken. Recover the hands underwater close to the body, as in a breaststroke pullout, take several more kicks, and repeat.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Focuses on head movement.
how: This drill is similar to the Biondi Drill but focuses on moving the head from near-full extension with the chin forward to a flexed position with the chin close to the chest. During the underwater pull, keep the chin extended forward and remain close to the waterline, lifting only enough to breathe. The motion resembles gliding across the surface. After a very short pause, bring the chin toward the chest and recover the arms to the starting position. Move slowly. Use fins if the kick is not strong enough.

warnings.reason: Repeatedly moving the chin from near-maximal extension toward the chest may cause cervical hyperextension and flexion. The neck range should be reduced and controlled.

purpose_text: Focuses on the end of the pull and correct underwater hand position.
how: This is a version of the Biondi Drill with a shorter arm movement. Begin with the arms in a diamond shape, with the elbows and hands aligned with the shoulders when viewed from the side, and push past the hips with a timed kick. Dorsiflex the hands, and direct the water backward rather than upward at the end of the pull. Recover the hands underwater. Use a snorkel to reduce the need to lift the head for breathing.

warnings.reason: The instruction to dorsiflex the hands does not clearly identify the intended wrist direction, and its propulsive effect may not align with standard butterfly instruction. The wrist position should be clarified and reviewed.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Flattens the stroke and develops rhythm and tempo. It also helps keep the head and shoulders low during breathing and encourages a quick, controlled return of the head to the water.
how: Swim butterfly with a freestyle kick. Use fins for assistance. The freestyle kick provides more continuous propulsion and reduces excessive vertical movement, helping the swimmer experience a flatter butterfly stroke.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops timing and stroke length.
how: Swim butterfly at a considerably reduced speed. This drill is recommended for experienced swimmers with sufficient shoulder strength to maintain proper form.

warnings.reason: Very slow butterfly can reduce momentum and increase shoulder loading. Use only with swimmers who can maintain form, and limit repetition distance and fatigue.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Allows younger swimmers to reset between strokes and focus on breathing after each complete butterfly stroke.
how: Take 1 butterfly stroke with 2 butterfly kicks, followed by 2 butterfly kicks in streamline.

purpose_text: DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Develops early vertical forearm (EVF) and maintenance of the catch, preventing the elbows from dropping or leading. Appropriate for more experienced swimmers.
how: Swim butterfly with closed fists. Use fins. This requires greater attention to the forearms rather than the hands.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Connects the single-arm drill to the full stroke and supports a high-arm recovery.
how: Pull with one arm, then the other arm, and then both arms together. Keep the resting hand in front during the single-arm pulls. Variations include taking several consecutive pulls or performing 2-3 pulls with each arm separately followed by 1 full stroke, or the reverse. Breathe to the side during single-arm strokes to practice a flatter position, and breathe to the front during full strokes. The drill also allows younger swimmers to complete longer butterfly sets.

name_en: HEAD UP BUTTERFLY WITH FLUTTER KICK aka. “TARZAN” FLY
purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Allows observation of hand-entry position and the beginning of the catch. This is an advanced drill focused specifically on that portion of the stroke.
how: Swim butterfly while keeping the head above the water. Fins provide substantial assistance. This is useful for swimmers whose arms enter too narrowly or too widely. Use the drill sparingly; its purpose is to show the swimmer where the hands enter and develop awareness of that position.

warnings.reason: Keeping the head continuously above water during butterfly may increase strain on the neck, lower back, and shoulders. Restrict the drill to short repetitions and appropriate swimmers.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Works on keeping the hips high and the chin low during the breath.
how: Swim butterfly with or without fins while breathing to the side. Alternate sides.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Focuses on a smooth, controlled, and quiet butterfly recovery.
how: Use a flutter kick with fins. Complete a butterfly pull from front to back, pause at the end of the pull, and then slowly recover the straight arms forward. This is a slow-motion practice of the recovery phase.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Demonstrates how timing develops at the beginning of the pull.
how: Perform a full-body butterfly movement at the surface while sculling only in front with the hands. Press the chest downward during the outsweep scull, and allow the body to rise during the insweep scull.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Improves timing, kick power, and stroke length.
how: Perform three (3) kicks at the beginning of the stroke, and then begin the pull while applying a strong 4th kick as the hands move under the body. This sets up a relaxed recovery and moves the body forward. The drill resembles the Lazy Butterfly drill, but emphasizes the timing and power of the kick at the end of the pull.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Teaches a vertical, straight-arm recovery.
how: Pull with the right arm, both arms, the left arm, and both arms, keeping the arms straight during recovery. Breathe to the side during single-arm pulls and to the front during full pulls.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops forward body elevation and provides a substitute for full butterfly during sets for younger swimmers.
how: Perform 2 butterfly strokes and 2 breaststroke strokes while maintaining the dolphin kick throughout. Younger swimmers often enjoy this drill. Fins may be used.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Introduces the undulating movement used in butterfly.
how: Swim freestyle with dolphin kicks. Use 1 kick per stroke so that each arm entry is paired with a kick.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. A dryland exercise that demonstrates wrist-led arm recovery.
how: Stand upright with the arms at the sides. Draw the shoulder blades together, keep the elbows extended so that the arms remain straight, and raise the arms overhead from behind with relaxed wrists and the fingers pointing downward. Finish with the fingers pointing toward the ceiling, or stop when the arms reach overhead. Repeat while bent at the waist, and later add the head movement. The exercise may also be performed in shallow water.

warnings.reason: A dryland movement performed with locked elbows from behind the body to overhead may provoke shoulder impingement in swimmers with limited mobility. Screen range of motion and avoid forcing the position.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Helps control excessive undulation or chest pressure because downward shoulder flexion is more difficult with the little fingers raised.
how: Perform dolphin kick with the little fingers raised above the water and the arms straight from the elbows. Use a snorkel to avoid lifting the head and to focus on the movement.

purpose_text: BEGINNER, DETAIL. Helps young swimmers use the kick to support breathing in butterfly and encourages coordinated chest and hip action.
how: With the arms at the sides, take 1 breath and 1 kick. Return the forehead quickly toward the water, with the chin toward the chest, after breathing, and direct the face toward the wall as the breath begins. Pause for 2 seconds and repeat. The coach should ensure that the body continues moving forward throughout the kick and breath. Use fins.

warnings.reason: Rapidly drawing the chin toward the chest and driving the face toward the wall may create an overly head-led butterfly action. The intended timing and movement source should be reviewed.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Helps young swimmers develop stroke power and timing.
how: In shallow water, have swimmers simulate jumping rope while using a butterfly pull to move across the pool. The goal is to press downward with the palms while jumping upward, practicing the timing of the first kick and the end of the pull.

warnings.reason: Jumping and pulling in shallow water may create slipping, ankle or knee impact, and collision risks. Use a clear area, appropriate depth, and direct supervision.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Exaggerates the dolphin undulation to develop awareness of stroke rhythm and full-range head movement. This advanced drill may be useful for older or larger young swimmers who have difficulty with butterfly.
how: Reach the arms and face upward during recovery and look toward the hands. Drive the body upward as described, and then dive forward as the hands extend in front and the chin moves toward the chest. Drive the hips toward the surface and travel deeper underwater. Repeat after resurfacing. Use fins.

warnings.reason: Deliberately exaggerating head movement and body amplitude may increase cervical and lumbar stress. Limit the range and ensure controlled whole-body coordination.
Rising as high as possible before diving deeply creates water-depth, breath-holding, and pool-bottom collision risks. Adequate depth, spacing, and direct supervision are required.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Teaches undulation to young swimmers who are beginning butterfly and provides an engaging variation.
how: Instead of using a kick to reach upward as in the Super Dolphin Drill, push from the bottom in shallow water to perform a dolphin dive and resurface. Emphasize a simultaneous downward arm push at the sides while jumping upward to gain height before diving hands-first with the head down. Keep the arms straight and the wrists relaxed during the overhead movement. Progress gradually from height to distance.

warnings.reason: Jumping explosively from the pool bottom and entering head-first in shallow water creates a substantial bottom- and surface-impact risk. Use only where depth and direct supervision make the progression safe.

purpose_text: DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Develops feel for the water during the pull, early vertical forearm (EVF), a flat pull path, and correction of short pulls or early recovery.
how: Begin in a relaxed prone float with the arms above the head, palms down, and hands shoulder-width apart. Complete the butterfly pull and stop as the hands reach the surface beside the hips, with the palms up and the arms fully extended while the head remains neutral. Maintain the glide and try to travel farther on each repetition. A breath may be taken.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Develops an undulating rhythm for younger swimmers.
how: The swimmer wears a snorkel and holds one end of a pole while face-down in streamline. The coach holds the opposite end and walks along the pool edge, assisting the undulating movement by moving the pole up and down in the intended rhythm.

warnings.reason: A coach pushing and pulling a pole from the deck creates risks of grip loss, contact with the swimmer's face or shoulder, and a fall from the deck. Equipment control and coach positioning must be reviewed.

purpose_text: DETAIL, APPRECIATION. Teaches late-breath timing, in which the head remains underwater slightly longer to reduce drag before breathing. Swimmers should already perform regular butterfly with consistent technique.
how: Swim butterfly with fins. Keep the head underwater until the end of the pull, and take a quick breath as the arms recover overhead. Return the head to the water as the hands enter and the downward kick finishes. Use a quick, controlled head movement so that the head and arm action support forward body movement. Briefly glide in streamline to feel the forward surge.

warnings.reason: The instruction that the head and arms pull the body forward, together with the prescribed late-breath timing, may not suit every swimmer's rhythm. The intended coordination should be reviewed individually.

purpose_text: Helps young swimmers learn the start step by step.
how:
Maintain a tight streamline with the arms pressing against the sides of the head during each step.
1. Sit on the edge with the feet in the water, and dive.
2. Kneel, and dive.
3. Kneel on one leg with the other foot in front, and dive.
4. Dive from the edge with either the feet together or a staggered foot position.
5. Repeat from the starting blocks.
Repeat the steps from the block as needed.

warnings.reason: Every diving progression requires confirmation of permitted water depth, starting-block rules, supervisor placement, and whether head-first entry is allowed at the facility.

purpose_text: Helps drive the arms forward and carry the body into the dive.
how: Perform a start with the hands near the hips, similar to a cowboy preparing to draw.

purpose_text: Teaches the swimmer to drive the head forward to develop additional speed from the coupling motion.
how: During the dive, briefly look toward a board held by someone 15-20 yards down the lane. The board color may be changed, and young swimmers may identify the color after completing the start.

warnings.reason: Looking toward a distant target during entry may disrupt head position and entry angle. Use only when depth, target placement, and swimmer skill allow the head to remain safely aligned.

purpose_text: Helps with arm speed.
how: Raise the hands toward the ceiling with the elbows bent. Drive the hands forward during the dive.

purpose_text: Practices a wide arm swing rather than a direct forward movement only.
how: Perform a start. Immediately after leaving the block, extend the arms outward to the sides and return them to streamline before entering the water.

warnings.reason: Spreading the arms after leaving the block and returning to streamline before entry may increase the risk of an uncontrolled or misaligned entry. Restrict the drill to skilled swimmers under direct supervision.

purpose_text: For young swimmers who have difficulty progressing from seated or kneeling dives to a squat start, or who jump flat from the blocks. Helps them experience a head-first streamlined entry.
how: Place a large exercise ball beside the pool. Have the swimmer lie with the lower abdomen supported on the ball and assume a streamline position. With the swimmer’s consent, support the waist while standing over the swimmer, and roll the swimmer into the water.

warnings.reason: Rolling a swimmer from a large exercise ball beside the pool creates substantial fall, head-impact, and coach-lifting risks. The setup and physical assistance method require formal safety review.

purpose_text: Provides more time in the air to observe body position and achieve a streamlined entry with the hips flexed.
how: Take a step on the block with the arms overhead, circle the arms backward, and then drive them forward from below. If the facility and conditions permit, take several running steps beside the block and dive using the same arm action.

warnings.reason: Running on a wet pool deck or performing a running dive beside the block creates a high risk of slipping and collision. Facility permission and a dedicated, dry approach area are required.

purpose_text: Reinforces a clean entry and an efficient streamline.
how: Perform a start and then float as far as possible without additional propulsion. Some swimmers can travel a full short-course length from the dive alone.

purpose_text: Balance.
how: Balance on the front leg, raise the rear leg, and perform the dive.

warnings.reason: Diving from a one-leg balance position may increase block-slip and asymmetric-entry risk. Use only with skilled swimmers under direct supervision.

purpose_text: Teaches entry through a single, narrow opening.
how: Place 2 pool noodles across the lane several feet apart. The swimmer dives between them without touching either noodle. Gradually reduce the space as appropriate.

warnings.reason: Diving between floating noodles requires control of noodle movement, adjacent-lane traffic, entry depth, and clear landing space. Direct supervision is required.

purpose_text: Develops height and distance during the dive and practices a head-first entry for smaller children. The challenge may increase engagement.
how: An instructor holds the noodle in front of and above the water while the swimmer dives over it without contact.

warnings.reason: Diving over a noodle held by another person creates contact and entry-angle risks. Maintain adequate clearance, water depth, and a controlled holding position.

purpose_text: Develops coordination as the hands pull first and then move forward. Also isolates the leg action so that it can be felt more clearly.
how: In the starting position, hold 1 buoy in each hand and toss the buoys backward while leaving the block.

warnings.reason: Throwing buoys backward while leaving the block may strike swimmers, coaches, or deck users behind the start. A completely clear rear area and controlled equipment collection are required.

purpose_text: Promotes a firm water entry with the legs and feet together. Useful for young swimmers who spread or cross the legs during a dive.
how: Dive with a buoy between the legs and try to retain it. Progress from the thighs to the knees and then to the ankles.

warnings.reason: Holding a buoy progressively closer to the ankles during a dive may restrict balance correction and leg separation after entry. The placement and release method require safety review.

purpose_text: Dryland. Develops feel for hand extension and different finishing angles.
how: Practice several hand-extension angles with a Vasa trainer or resistance cords. This can be performed during or between other dryland exercises.

purpose_text: Uses paddles to improve awareness of hand and wrist position during finishes.
how: Use paddles to perform several finish repetitions.

purpose_text: Teaches young swimmers who have never performed a flip turn, beginning with the basic movement.
how:
1. Standing somersault: Stand with the hands beside the thighs, jump upward from the pool bottom, and perform a compact somersault by tucking the chin toward the chest and allowing the legs to travel overhead. Land on the feet again. Move without rushing. It is acceptable for the slightly bent legs to return slowly toward the bottom.
2. Horizontal somersault: In the middle of the pool, swim several strokes. Pull the leading arm to the side just before the turn, and allow the legs to travel overhead. Keep the arms in place without spreading them; linking the thumbs may help keep the arms together and encourage use of the core. Finish on the back in a straight streamline with the arms overhead. Practice either after several strokes or from a float with one arm extended, pulling it back before the somersault. Alternate the leading arm between repetitions.
3. Somersault at the wall: Begin 1 arm’s length from the wall and apply the same principles as in Step 2, placing the feet on the wall approximately 1 foot underwater. Finish on the back with the knees bent at a 90-degree angle for push-off.
4. Push off on the back: Point the toes toward the ceiling when the feet contact the wall, and remain on the back for the dolphin kicks.
5. Rotate to the stomach after push-off: Rotate after leaving the wall rather than while on the wall, and float as far as possible. This applies to the freestyle flip turn. For backstroke, remain on the back and float in streamline.
6. Perform several underwater dolphin kicks immediately after push-off while rotating to the stomach, and begin flutter kicking at breakout. For backstroke, remain on the back and perform the dolphin kicks.
7. Time the first recovery so that it begins as the head and shoulders break the surface. The first catch and pull begin before that point. Do not breathe on the first pull.

warnings.reason: Jumping from the pool bottom into a somersault requires direct control of water depth, bottom traction, and head and neck position.

purpose_text: Teaches young swimmers to make a compact turn with the upper body and provides support while the legs travel overhead in a straighter path.
how: Perform a somersault over a lane line in the shallow end. Place the arms over the line with the palms down, pull both arms backward, and rotate over the lane line while keeping the chin and chest close to it. Allow the legs to travel over and enter the water on the opposite side. Coaches may assist by guiding the legs over the line.

warnings.reason: Turning over a lane line while a coach pushes the legs creates entrapment, collision, and excessive-assistance risks. The lane setup and manual assistance method must be controlled.

purpose_text: Performed in the shallow end for smaller children and in the deep end for more experienced swimmers.
how: Perform simulated flip turns from standing or while sculling. Gradually move closer to the wall so that swimmers become comfortable without fear of contact.

warnings.reason: Progressing flips increasingly close to the wall requires a defined approach distance to prevent head, heel, or foot contact with the wall.

name_en: FLIP IN THE MIDDLE aka. 3 STROKES AND FLIP
purpose_text: Allows more turn repetitions within each pool length.
how: While swimming easy freestyle or backstroke, perform a somersault every 10 yards, in the middle of each length, and at the end.

purpose_text: Encourages a compact body position and teaches the somersault movement.
how: Use a pool noodle as an obstacle for the somersault, either from a standing position or while kicking toward the wall with the noodle under the armpits. To keep the noodle in place, the swimmer must form a compact position around it. Losing the noodle during push-off is acceptable.

warnings.reason: Wrapping the body around a noodle during a flip can allow the neck or arms to become caught against the noodle or nearby lane equipment. Direct supervision is required.

purpose_text: Helps smaller children rotate directly over the body rather than sideways and learn to turn without using the arms.
how: Hold the noodle with both hands in front and rotate over it without releasing the noodle, either at the wall or in open water. Push off in streamline.

purpose_text: Progresses from the Noodle Flip 2 drill.
how: Hold the noodle below the abdomen with both hands near the hips. Perform a somersault and finish in streamline.

purpose_text: Reinforces the correct push-off for smaller children who surface immediately after the turn.
how: Hold a noodle at the surface near the flags, or closer if needed. Swimmers pass over it before the wall and travel underneath it after push-off. Begin close to the wall so that the swimmer initiates the turn as the chest reaches the noodle; then move the noodle progressively farther away to teach underwater dolphin kicking and streamline after the wall.

warnings.reason: Beginning the flip as the chest contacts the noodle may bring the equipment into the face or neck. Noodle placement, firmness, and release must be controlled.

purpose_text: Corrects foot contact that is too high or too low on the wall.
how: Hold a kickboard against the wall approximately 6-8 inches underwater from the top edge. Swimmers approach with several yards of speed and try to contact the board with the feet at the target area. Contact with the softer board provides feedback.

warnings.reason: Striking a kickboard fixed against the wall with the feet may cause toe or ankle impact and board displacement. Use a soft target, controlled speed, and secure positioning.

purpose_text: Reinforces streamline after push-off and immediate kicking.
how: Perform 10-yard underwater dolphin-kick sprints on the back from the wall, beginning the kick immediately at push-off. Rotate so that the body reaches the stomach by the time it surfaces. Return to the wall and repeat.

warnings.reason: A 10-yard underwater dolphin segment should be reviewed alongside the 15-meter underwater limit that applies to relevant competition strokes, as well as pool depth and breath-holding controls.

purpose_text: Helps prevent the arms from moving outward while the legs travel overhead. Particularly useful with younger swimmers.
how: Float or use a light flutter kick while holding 2 boards at the sides, 1 in each hand. Perform a somersault; the boards limit outward arm movement and should finish near or above the shoulders.

purpose_text: A variation of the 2 Boards Flip drill. Slows the movement, teaches core use, and limits unnecessary hand and arm action.
how: Hold 2 kickboards or pull buoys in front and flutter-kick toward the wall. Just before the equipment reaches the wall, move the arms outward and perform the somersault while bringing the boards together for a push-off on the back.

purpose_text: Practices both freestyle and backstroke versions of the flip turn in the same drill.
how: Swim 1 length freestyle, perform a flip turn, and swim 1 length on the back. Repeat continuously.

purpose_text: Focuses on establishing streamline.
how: Pause for a count of 3 when the feet contact the wall.

purpose_text: Helps the swimmer rotate in a straight line and push off on the back.
how: The coach holds 2 parallel boards partially submerged, forming a narrow corridor. The swimmer turns without contacting the boards with the feet and pushes off on the back.

warnings.reason: A coach holding boards underwater to create a turning corridor may cause hand-foot contact or board displacement. Board placement and safe release must be planned.

purpose_text: Allows multiple turns in succession so that the swimmer can focus on turning rather than swimming distance.
how: Swim 3-4 strokes away from the wall, perform a somersault in open water, swim back, and perform a flip turn at the wall. Repeat as needed. This creates a shortened length with 1 open-water somersault and 1 wall turn.

purpose_text: Develops rapid knee movement toward the chest while maintaining greater knee extension during the initial leg path.
how: Perform a V-sit scull on the back. Then tuck the knees quickly, rotate over the heels to the stomach, and begin sprinting. The goal is to improve the speed and compactness of the somersault. The lower legs remain relatively straight as they travel through the water.

warnings.reason: Explosively tucking and rotating from a V-sit may load the lower back, hamstrings, and neck. Apply only to swimmers with adequate strength and mobility and limit fatigue.

purpose_text: Develops entry and exit speed. Warning: This drill is not permitted in some pools, and the deck may be slippery. Perform it only with experienced, well-coordinated swimmers.
how: Run several feet along the side of the pool, dive so that the swimmer is prepared to turn upon surfacing at speed, perform the flip turn, and push diagonally beneath the lane lines or straight down the lane.

warnings.reason: A running dive from the pool deck has a very high slipping and head-impact risk and may be prohibited by the facility. Do not use without explicit facility approval and strict controls.
Pushing diagonally beneath lane lines after a dive-turn may create collision with lane equipment or swimmers in adjacent lanes. Use only in a closed, dedicated area.

purpose_text: Race-speed turn drill and breath control.
how: Take 4 strokes without breathing into the wall, perform 3 dolphin kicks after push-off, and take 2 strokes before breathing.

warnings.reason: Prescribed breath restriction before and after the wall may create hypoxic stress. The pattern should be adapted to individual ability and stopped immediately if symptoms occur.

purpose_text: Increases turn speed through a friendly competitive activity.
how:
Use 2 swimmers. One starts at the 5m mark and the other at the 7m mark, or several meters apart according to ability. Both face away from the turning end. At the whistle, both swimmers somersault; the swimmer at 5m attempts to touch the wall before being tagged by the swimmer who started at 7m. Use no more than 2 swimmers per lane. For smaller children, 2 groups may be positioned on opposite sides of the lanes.

This drill may also be used for open turns.

warnings.reason: A chase-and-tag turn drill creates collision risk within the same lane. Starting gaps, lane direction, swimmer pairing, and the maximum number of participants must be strictly controlled.

purpose_text: Helps swimmers press the head and chest downward into the turn and reduces reliance on circular hand movements.
how: Interlace the hands behind the head and kick toward the wall. Press the hands and head into the turn, and then move the hands quickly into streamline.

warnings.reason: Approaching and turning with the hands interlaced behind the head limits head protection and delays movement into streamline. Use only with controlled speed and direct supervision.

purpose_text: Includes 3 turns over approximately 60 yards and also supports individual-medley transition-turn practice.
how: Start at the flags, perform a turn, swim 25, perform a turn, swim 25, perform a turn, and finish at the flags.

purpose_text: Addresses slow rolling flip turns and the belief that the swimmer must be on the stomach at push-off. It also develops the palm press and rapid transition to streamline. Practicing away from the wall may reduce fear of contact. Emphasizing a forceful leg movement can develop power in the somersault.
how: Float face-down with the arms at the sides and the palms down. Perform the somersault by pressing the palms downward and using the core to drive the legs overhead quickly, finishing in streamline while floating on the back.

purpose_text: Simulates race pace.
how: Begin standing on or slightly behind the T in the shallow end. Jump upward from the pool bottom and enter the flip turn. After the turn, sprint to the halfway mark with a strong underwater phase and breakout, and then swim easily back in the adjacent lane so that the next swimmer can practice in the center of the lane.

warnings.reason: Explosively jumping from the bottom in shallow water and connecting the motion to a turn may create ankle, knee, and wall-impact risks. Depth, distance, and landing control are required.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL. Develops balance, body rotation, and swimming predominantly on the sides.
how: Take 3 strokes, and then balance on the side for 6 kicks with one arm extended forward and the other upper arm raised vertically to 90 degrees. The forearm may hang near the goggles, remain straight, or use an intermediate recovery position according to the sprint or distance style being practiced. After 6 kicks, switch sides with 3 strokes. Keep the head stable and aligned, with the eyes directed toward the bottom, and rotate the body fully. During the kick, keep the shoulder of the raised arm out of the water and extend the other arm forward with the palm down. Use a snorkel or fins for assistance if needed. Switch slowly to develop accurate rotation, and switch more quickly to practice driving the hand forward over the water.

purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Teaches early vertical forearm (EVF) by practicing movement of the fingers and hand before movement of the upper arm.
how: Practice the catch and pull over a lane line while using paddles. Lie flat in the water with the arms over the lane line and the elbows aligned with it to feel the beginning of the catch cycle. Repeat as needed.

warnings.reason: Using paddles while performing a catch over the lane line creates finger-entrapment, paddle-snagging, and lane-tension risks. The lane should be isolated and the equipment carefully controlled.

name_en: ONE HAND WALL PUSH (WITH LOW CEILING)
purpose_text: DETAIL, BEGINNER. Develops head position and side breathing.
how: Kick while holding the wall with 1 hand and keeping the other hand at the side, and practice breathing to the side. Coaches can observe from the deck and guide the head position by hand, or place a flat kickboard slightly above the head and water surface so that the swimmer breathes beneath it.

warnings.reason: Guiding the swimmer's head by hand or placing a kickboard immediately above the head may cause neck or facial contact. Non-contact feedback should be preferred.

purpose_text: PROGRESSION, BEGINNER. Develops a quick breath without lingering and teaches exhalation into the water before inhalation.
how: This progression is suitable for beginners. Begin by practicing quick breaths while standing in the shallow end with the face in the water, and then progress through kicking exercises. The breath should be taken promptly after exhaling while the face is submerged. Many young swimmers hold the breath underwater and then attempt to exhale and inhale above the water at the same time, which disrupts stroke continuity.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Focuses on side balance, stroke extension, and rotation.
how: This is a simpler variation of 3 Strokes + 6 Kicks. Take 1 stroke to switch arms, and then perform 6 kicks on the side with one arm extended forward and the other arm raised vertically; the recovering forearm may be bent, straight, or in an intermediate position. Breathe as needed by rotating the head to the side and returning it to neutral. Fins and a snorkel make the drill easier. Begin with slow switches to refine the movement, and then increase speed for race-pace practice. Remain on the side while kicking and control the rotation speed.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL. Develops correct movement at speed, particularly for a galloping stroke rhythm.
how: Begin with one arm extended forward and the other arm at the side. Complete 1 full stroke cycle with both arms, perform it quickly, and then pause for 6 kicks. Begin the next length with the other arm extended.

warnings.reason: A galloping stroke rhythm may be appropriate only for certain swimmers, events, and tactical goals. It should not be presented as a universal freestyle technique.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, DETAIL, BEGINNER. Teaches a high-elbow position by allowing the swimmer to see and feel the movement of one arm.
how: Pull with 1 arm while the other remains extended in front. Rotate the body with each pull. Complete 1 length with one arm and the next length with the other. Focus on early vertical forearm (EVF) and high-elbow recovery.

purpose_text: BEGINNER. Develops patience, balance, and attention to the complete stroke.
how: Allow the hands to meet in front while swimming, with a small space between them. Perform 6 kicks between strokes to practice breathing timing. The drill may also be performed while holding a kickboard or another object. A snorkel and fins may be used.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION, DETAIL. Teaches the swimmer to establish the catch with the entire forearm rather than the hand alone and encourages a high underwater elbow from the beginning of the stroke.
how: Swim while holding tennis or table-tennis balls, or make a complete fist rather than curling only the fingers. A pull buoy may be used for additional effect. Perform the drill without rushing. It may feel slow, but returning to open hands should make the difference in propulsion more noticeable.

purpose_text: DETAIL, ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Develops a high-elbow recovery for efficient longer-distance swimming.
how: During freestyle recovery, touch the armpit on each stroke or slide the thumb along the body from the hip toward the head. As an alternative, drag the fingers lightly on the water during recovery. Emphasize body rotation to reduce shoulder stress, and keep the forearm and wrist relaxed during recovery.

warnings.reason: Touching the armpit and exaggerating body roll may provoke shoulder impingement or excessive rotation. Limit the recovery path to a comfortable, pain-free range.

The contrast between straight-arm recovery for rotational or centrifugal effects and bent-arm recovery for distance efficiency is athlete-dependent. The technical claim should be reviewed before general use.

purpose_text: DETAIL. Develops balance, water posture, arm entry, and timing. A variation of the ¾ catch-up drill.
how: Pause the recovering arm at 45 degrees with the fingers pointing toward the water in front. Keep the other arm extended forward to form the “bow and arrow” position. Switch arms with each stroke and pause with the opposite arm raised. Fins may be used; more advanced swimmers may perform the drill without fins to increase leg workload and maintain continuous kicking.

name_en: SINGLE ARM DRILL aka. ONE-ARMED BANDIT
purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Develops body rotation and increases reliance on the kick.
how:
Pull with 1 arm while the opposite arm remains at the side.
Breathe quickly to the side opposite the working arm as it reaches the shoulder line. Rotate the body while maintaining posture. Fins are recommended for younger swimmers.

purpose_text: ESSENTIAL, BEGINNER. Develops whole-body rotation and helps prevent a scissor kick.
how: Kick with both arms at the sides, and rotate the entire body, including the shoulders and hips, every 6 kicks. Keep the eyes directed toward the bottom unless breathing. Hold the head still while the body rotates from side to side. Fins or a snorkel may be used. Perform the rotation slowly or at increased speed.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops feel for the water.
how: Begin as in the Fist Drill. On each length, extend 1 additional finger until all 5 fingers are in the normal position; the progression takes 5-6 lengths. For the Bear Claw variation, keep the fingers spread and flexed.

purpose_text: APPRECIATION. Develops awareness of the connection between the hips and shoulders, the effect of water resistance, and forward reach as the body rotates to the side.
how: Swim full freestyle underwater. The drill is demanding underwater, but normal surface swimming may feel easier afterward. Fins make the drill more manageable.

warnings.reason: Swimming full freestyle underwater creates breath-holding and collision risks. Limit the distance, use a clear lane, and provide direct supervision.
